analysis.one_liner: Bans union contracts that require workers to join a union or pay union fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal labor law to repeal the parts of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that let union contracts require employees to join the union or pay union dues and fees as a condition of keeping their job. Today, if workers at a unionized workplace vote in a union and negotiate such a contract, everyone covered can be required to pay for the representation they receive. This bill would make that illegal nationwide. The bill was introduced by Senator Jesse Helms in May 2001, referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in unionized workplaces who do not want to join the union or pay dues would be able to keep their jobs and receive union representation without paying. Employers negotiating with unions would also benefit, because unions would have less money and fewer members to work with.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act that allow a union contract to require employees to join the union as a condition of employment.

It also repeals the parallel provision in the Railway Labor Act, including the part that lets railroads deduct union dues from paychecks under such contracts, so railroad and airline workers would be covered too.

Under federal law, a union that negotiates a contract must represent every worker in the bargaining unit, including workers who decline to join; this bill would make those workers free to receive that representation without paying dues or fees for it.

analysis.who_pays: Unions would lose dues from workers who choose not to pay, shrinking their budgets and membership rolls. Union members would bear the cost indirectly: a union that must represent everyone but can collect from fewer people has less power and money to bargain, which is why opponents argue such laws drive down the wages and benefits union workplaces win.

drawbacks.text: Because unions are legally required to bargain for every worker in the unit, the bill lets workers take the benefit of union representation without contributing to its cost; over time this shrinks union treasuries and rolls.

Weaker unions bargain for less: the durable finding from states with such laws is lower union membership and lower wages in unionized workplaces, so the individual 'choice' comes at the price of the collective bargaining power that produced the pay and benefits in the first place.

The bill would also apply to railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act, striking their special provision for union dues payroll deduction, dismantling arrangements those industries have operated under for decades.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The individual-freedom argument is real: nobody loves being told to pay dues to an organization they did not vote for. But the bill's design creates a straightforward free-rider problem: unions must represent everyone but could collect from almost no one, and the well-documented result elsewhere is smaller, poorer unions and lower pay in the workplaces they cover. On balance, the cost to workers' collective bargaining power outweighs the individual choice it grants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight from introduction to the Senate committee that handles labor law and sat there; no hearing, no vote, and no floor action ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jesse Helms introduced the bill on May 14, 2001, joined by three Senate Republicans as original co-sponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Six Republican senators signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organized labor and the workers it represents: because the bill never advanced, the national ban on union-security agreements was never enacted, and union contracts requiring dues remain lawful.

for.name: Sen. Jesse Helms
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Strom Thurmond, Tim Hutchinson, and Bob Smith
for.what_they_did: Joined Helms as original co-sponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 6 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die there.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — seven senators in all, none of the 49 Senate Democrats — and the bill received no action in the labor committee, which was chaired by a Democrat for the Congress.

industries.note: The bill repeals the legal basis for contracts requiring union membership and dues, so unions would lose dues revenue and members while still being required to represent every worker. Their loss of bargaining power falls on the same people the unions negotiate for.

Employers would negotiate with unions that are smaller and poorer, since workers could keep their jobs without paying dues. The gain to employers comes at the expense of the workers' collective representation.
The Railway Labor Act provision struck by the bill lets rail carriers deduct union dues from paychecks under union-security agreements; repealing it weakens unions in these industries specifically.
